Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.

Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home.
I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, who am ever known for my cunning and my wandering.

‘Your next encounter will be with the Sirens, who bewitch everybody that approaches them. There is no homecoming for the man who draws near them unawares and hears the Sirens’ voices; no wife nor little child will ever stand by his side in gladness, but the Sirens sit in a meadow and beguile him with their melodious song. All round there is a great heap of bones, rotting bodies, and the skins shrink upon them.’

‘I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, who am always devising some new scheme, and my fame reaches heaven. I live in Ithaca, where there is a high mountain called Neriton, covered with forests; and there are many islands round it, Dulichium, Same, and Zacynthus. […] I am not going to tell you the whole story of my wanderings, for it would take too long; but I will tell you about the most famous and most eventful of my adventures.’
